title: The Decameron
author: Giovanni Boccaccio
description: The frame of the hundred tales, set in and just outside Florence in the plague year of 1348. The death-dealing pestilence empties the city; seven young ladies meet by chance in the church of Santa Maria Novella and resolve to flee; with three young men they retire two short miles into the hills toward Fiesole, to a villa traditionally identified with Poggio Gherardo; from there they wander to the secluded Valley of the Ladies; and at the end the company returns to Santa Maria Novella, whence it set out. The hundred tales roam all of Europe, but the setting the map fixes is this Florentine frame, the ground of the greatest book of the Italian Middle Ages.

route.summary: Boccaccio opens the frame with the plague of 1348 loose in Florence, the fairest of Italian cities, and gives one of the great eyewitness accounts of the Black Death: the plague-boils, the abandoned dead, the collapse of law and kinship. It is the ground the whole book flees from.

In the great Dominican church of Santa Maria Novella, all but empty in the plague, seven young noblewomen meet after Mass. The eldest, whom Boccaccio calls Pampinea, proposes that they leave the dying city for the country. The basilica still stands on its piazza near the western edge of the old city.

route.displayName: The villa in the hills (toward Fiesole)
route.summary: Two miles into the hills that climb toward Fiesole, the ten reach the villa where the first days of storytelling unfold, its courtyard and cold wells and wonder-goodly gardens set against the plague below. Here Dioneo, the merriest of the young men, sets the note of licensed pleasure for the whole retreat.
route.note: The text fixes the villa only as a palace on a little hill two short miles from Florence, unnamed. The pin sits on Villa di Poggio Gherardo, the fourteenth-century house in the hills toward Fiesole that Janet Ross and Edward Hutton identified as the company's first refuge; Villa Palmieri at San Domenico is the rival candidate. Both are inferences from the two-mile distance and the surviving medieval fabric, not a named place.

route.summary: At the close of the Sixth Day, Elisa leads the seven women, without the men, to a secret round valley ringed by six hills, with a clear lakelet at its centre where they bathe. It is Boccaccio's most perfect garden of retreat, a walled Eden a mile from the villa in the Fiesole hills.
route.note: The Valle delle Donne is described minutely but never located: a round plain ringed by six low hills, a mile or so from the villa. Tradition places it in the wooded folds below Fiesole toward Settignano and Maiano, near the Mensola stream under Poggio Gherardo; the pin sits there. It is a real-feeling but idealised valley, inferred from the hills of the frame rather than a mapped site.

route.summary: After ten days and a hundred tales the fortnight ends and the company rides back to Florence, taking leave in the same church of Santa Maria Novella where it first gathered. The frame closes exactly where it opened: the city survived, and the book is done.
